newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Party in Bunds to persist this week.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Party in Bunds to persist this week.

text.p: Investors who missed out on lucrative Bund spread plays last week can still cash in, analysts said on Monday, as ongoing EMU concerns and fears of a U.S. rate rise prompt further outperformance in the near term.

Even the prospect of Thursday's German employment report will do little to thwart spread widening, although signs of stronger economic growth by the end of the first quarter will likely call a halt to the bull trend. "There's likely to be good grounds for Bunds to push ahead a bit further over the week," said Ros Lifton at HSBC Markets.

"The markets are convinced we'll get weak data on the German employment front...which will reinforce the fundamental argument for Bunds. And there's the flight to quality if EMU is delayed," added Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC here.

Bund spreads with U.S. Treasuries and peripheral Europe ballooned last week after a hawkish congressional testimony from Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan and revived concerns of a delay to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) prompted a flight to safety.
The 10-year T-note/Bund spread widened 23 basis points over the week to 117 basis points on Friday.
BTPs also took a hammering against Bunds after Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said he thought it "possible" Germany would seek a delay to the start of Europe's planned single currency in 1999.
The ten-year BTP/Bund spread puffed out to 195 basis points from 165 at the beginning of the week. By 1300 GMT it was at 194 basis points after spiking over 200 earlier.
Despite this considerable move -- which meant all the BTP spread tightening of November, December and January was reversed in February -- more was still to come, analysts said.
"If we get a sustained breach of 200, that spread could go to 250 basis points quite quickly," said Michael Burke, senior economist at Citibank in London.
Lifton put 230 basis points as the peak.

"Italy's in a difficult position," she said. "If the currency weakens any more and we get all these concerns about Germany being compounded by domestic political concerns, there's a real chance the spread could spike out to 230."
Mark Fox, chief European strategist for fixed income at Lehman Brothers said a BTP/Bund spread of 220 basis points presented a good buying opportunity.
"That will probably be the peak...the worst of the damage is done now," he said.

Concern over an imminent U.S. rate rise means the Treasury/Bund spread also has further to widen. Lifton said it may billow out to 120 basis points near term, if Friday's payrolls data are disappointing for the market.
"If both non-farm payrolls and average hourly earnings are as robust as we expect, the market will be gunning for a rate hike as early as the March FOMC," Lifton said.
She estimates that payrolls will rise 325,000 in February, higher than the 237,000 Reuter consensus. The policy setting Federal Open Market Committee are due to meet on March 25.
Burke saw the Treasury/Bund spread widening to as much as 125 basis points. By 1300 GMT it was 115 basis points.
But with Bunds vulnerable to a knock within the next few months, analysts agreed spread plays rather than longer term curve plays were the order of the day.

"I don't expect German yields to fall on a continuous basis all year," said Burke. "Some of the recent orders and confidence data...suggest we might not be too far from a Bund damaging rebound in the economy."
Burke said investors piling into the safe hands of Bunds should head for the three to five year area.
"I wouldn't go any longer than that because there's likely to be a turnaround at some stage, whereas if anything, short rates will go lower," he said.

But Lifton was more sceptical. "I'd be somewhere between five and 10-years. "The short end isn't going to be the best position given the Bundesbank is getting quite a good amount of monetary easing through the exchange rate. I'm not sure the short end can make many gains on the economic data."
"But it's very much a short term play," she added. "With yields around 5.5 percent (on 10-years) I wouldn't take those positions on a longer term strategic play.
